an1.268:1.1: An “individual accomplished in view” is a stream-enterer. They might unthinkingly act as if something were permanent (etc.), but on reflection they would know that this is not the case. This is because they still have emotional responses due to desire, hate, and delusion, but not the wrong view of eternalism, etc. | These three chapters parallel [mn115:12.2]() ff., where someone who is “skilled in the possible and impossible” is qualified to make these statements.
an1.269:1.1: The teachings on impermanence (_anicca_) and suffering (_dukkha_) apply to all “conditions” (_saṅkhārā_), which means all phenomena produced by causes and productive of further causes.
an1.269:1.2: The teachings on impermanence (_anicca_) and suffering (_dukkha_) apply to all “conditions” (_saṅkhārā_), which means all phenomena produced by causes and productive of further causes.
an1.270:1.1: Not-self applies to all “things” (_dhammā_) which is broader than all “conditions”. The reason for this shift is not as obvious as one might like. I think the implication is that “all things” includes concepts, especially the Dhamma as a natural law. All things are impermanent; in the past they were impermanent; and in the future they will be impermanent. This doesn’t mean that the law of impermanence itself is permanent, for it is only a description (_paññatti_). But we can say that the statement “all conditions are impermanent” is always an accurate description of reality. Thus the law or principle of impermanence (_dhammaniyāmatā_, [an3.136:1.1]()) cannot be described as “impermanent”. Similar logic can be applied to suffering, the four noble truths, dependent origination, the eightfold path, and so on.
an1.271:1.1: Murder of mother, father, or an arahant, injuring a Buddha, and causing schism are said to be the five heinous deeds that result in rebirth in hell ([an5.129]()).
an1.276:1.1: A stream-enterer knows from their own experience that the Buddha’s teaching is both correct and liberating, so why would they dedicate themselves to another? | This is included with the previous five also at [an6.94:1.3](), and mentioned at [mn38:24.10]() and [sn16.11:8.3](). The six are perhaps also the things that cannot be done by a stream-enterer at [snp2.1:11.2]().
an1.277:1.1: A _lokadhātu_ is a single system with an earth, a sun and moon, planets, and a set of heavenly realms. Thus with due allowance for the different context, it is similar to a “solar system”. While many Buddhas may arise in the same solar system, they may not arise in the same region at the same time. There may, however, be many Buddhas simultaneously throughout the galaxy, an idea developed in later texts (eg. Mahāvastu 1.122).
